```{r}
#| label: numbers
## The few numbers the letter quotes, read from the same tables the manuscript
## reads, so the letter cannot drift from the paper.
root <- normalizePath(getwd())
while (!file.exists(file.path(root, "_quarto.yml")) && dirname(root) != root) root <- dirname(root)
rd <- function(p) read.csv(file.path(root, p), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
g_sig  <- rd("tag-seq/DESEQ_output/gonad/GONAD-SIG-DEG-apeglm.csv")
g_all  <- rd("tag-seq/DESEQ_output/gonad/GONAD-ALL-DEG-apeglm.csv")
l_sig  <- rd("tag-seq/DESEQ_output/liver/liver-SIG-DEG-apeglm.csv")
l_all  <- rd("tag-seq/DESEQ_output/liver/liver-ALL-DEG-apeglm.csv")
fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
up_pct <- round(100 * mean(g_sig$log2FoldChange > 0))
```

[[Date]]

[[Editor name]]\
Editor, *Molecular Ecology*

Dear [[Editor name]],

We submit our manuscript, "Gonadal but not hepatic transcriptomes distinguish
territorial from social sockeye salmon (*Oncorhynchus nerka*)", for
consideration as an Original Article in *Molecular Ecology*.

Adult salmon on the spawning grounds either defend territories or remain in
social aggregations, and the choice carries real energetic and reproductive
costs. Transcriptomic work on behavioural phenotype in fish has focused almost
entirely on the brain, so how that choice is expressed in peripheral tissues of
wild adults is largely unknown. We used 3′-tag RNA sequencing of gonad and
liver from territorial and social sockeye to ask which tissue carries the
phenotype.

The answer is clear-cut. The gonad differed markedly between phenotypes, with
`r fmt(nrow(g_sig))` of `r fmt(nrow(g_all))` tested genes differentially
expressed, `r up_pct`% of them higher in territorial fish. These genes form a
coherent programme of elevated translation and oxidative phosphorylation,
alongside strong induction of acute-phase genes. The liver, by contrast,
differed at only `r fmt(nrow(l_sig))` of `r fmt(nrow(l_all))` genes, with no
enriched pathway. The results point to reproductive investment, rather than
hepatic energy metabolism, as the physiological axis along which behavioural
type varies in spawning sockeye, and they identify candidate genes for testing
whether gonadal state drives behaviour or follows it.

We think the work suits *Molecular Ecology* because it uses a
transcriptomic approach to address a question in behavioural and reproductive
ecology in a wild population, and because it adds a peripheral-tissue
perspective to a literature dominated by neural gene expression. It also
includes a methodological point of general use for 3′-tag data: the
transcript-length correction commonly applied in enrichment testing is
inappropriate for this assay, and in our data it either removed the result or
failed without warning.

Every number, table and figure in the manuscript is produced by a scripted,
version-pinned analysis that is re-executed from a clean environment on each
change to the repository. Raw reads are deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read
Archive ([[BioProject accession]]), and the code and processed data are
archived at Zenodo ([[DOI]]).

This manuscript is not under consideration elsewhere, and all authors have
approved its submission. [[State any preprint, or delete this sentence.]]
